title: Evaporation and crystallisation: getting salt back
examples: How do you get salt back from salt water?
Why not boil the water dry?

explain.say: Have you ever seen a white crust on your skin after swimming in the sea? That is salt, left behind when the water dried. Look at the board. We start with salt dissolved in water. Let us get the salt back.

explain.say: See the flame? You heat the solution gently in a dish. The water evaporates, which means it turns into vapour and floats away. The salt cannot evaporate, so it stays. Where does the water go?

stages.label: Stop at half
stages.ask: Why do you only heat until half the water is gone?

explain.say: Into the air! Now look at this step. You stop heating when about half the water is gone and tiny crystals appear at the edge. If you boil it dry, the salt can spit and crack. Can you see why patience helps?

stages.label: Stop at half
stages.ask: Why do you only heat until half the water is gone?

explain.say: Look at the clock. As the solution cools slowly, the salt particles line up in neat repeating patterns and grow into crystals. A crystal is a solid with a regular shape. Slower cooling makes bigger crystals. Which would you rather see?

explain.say: Well done! Here you can compare the two ways. Boiling it all dry is quick but gives tiny bits. Slow crystallisation gives big, neat, pure crystals. Wow: salt makers in Gujarat in India and Guérande in France let the sun do this in huge shallow pans.

faq.a: Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas at its surface. When you heat salt water, the water evaporates away and the salt is left behind.

faq.q: Why do you only heat until half the water is gone?
faq.a: If you boil it dry, the salt can spit out of the dish and form tiny powdery bits. Stopping early and cooling slowly gives bigger, purer crystals.
As a saturated solution cools or loses water, not all the dissolved particles can stay dissolved. They join on in neat, repeating patterns, building a crystal.
Seawater is let into wide, shallow ponds called salt pans. The sun and wind evaporate the water, and the salt crystals are raked up.
asks: Where does table salt come from?

faq.q: What is the difference between evaporation and crystallisation?
faq.a: Evaporating to dryness removes all the water quickly and gives small powdery bits. Crystallisation removes some water, then lets the solution cool slowly, giving larger, purer crystals.

facts: Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid from a solution by evaporating some of the solvent and letting the solution cool so crystals form.
Slower cooling of a solution generally gives larger crystals.
